description: We are here to create. Here to make a difference.
summary:
We developed Sunline, an interactive web application that enables users to assess and compare lunar south pole landing sites and dates by analyzing two critical factors for any mission: solar energy availability and direct communication with Earth.
The tool combines digital elevation models from NASA's LRO/LOLA mission with high-precision astronomical ephemerides to reconstruct the lunar topographic horizon and calculate the visibility of the Sun and Earth from any selected location and point in time.
Through 3D visualizations, illumination maps, comparative analyses, and a date planner, Sunline transforms large volumes of scientific data into accessible information, helping users evaluate the feasibility of different mission scenarios.
Its significance lies in the fact that, at the lunar south pole, small variations in location or timing can determine whether a mission has access to solar power and communication with Earth or faces extended periods of darkness. Sunline makes these critical mission-planning variables accessible to researchers, mission designers, students, and space exploration enthusiasts through an intuitive and easy-to-use interactive tool.
details:
The Challenge and the Problem

The lunar south pole is a region of great interest for future space missions, but it presents significant operational challenges. Due to the low apparent elevation of the Sun and Earth, the terrain can obstruct solar illumination and communications for extended periods.

These conditions vary significantly even between locations separated by just a few hundred meters and change over time. As a result, a suitable landing site may no longer be viable if a launch is delayed.

The challenge is to facilitate the identification of suitable sites and time windows for future missions.

Sunline addresses this problem by integrating topographic and astronomical data to visualize, analyze, and compare the operational conditions of different lunar landing scenarios.

What Does Sunline Do and How Does It Work?

Sunline allows users to assess whether a lunar mission at a given location and date will have sufficient solar illumination and direct communication with Earth. It combines real scientific data with geometric and astronomical models, running all simulations directly in the browser without relying on external servers.

Its operation consists of four stages:

1. Astronomical Calculations: Uses Astronomy Engine and the IAU 2015 lunar orientation model / Archinal et al. (2018), incorporating 13 physical libration terms and topocentric parallax corrections for Earth. Results are cross-checked against NASA JPL Horizons.

2. Topographic Reconstruction: Processes NASA LRO/LOLA digital elevation models using Ray Marching, reconstructing the full 360° horizon up to 220 km while accounting for lunar curvature. It uses resolutions of up to 80 m/pixel in areas of interest and 240 m/pixel across the remaining covered region.

3. Illumination and Communication Calculations: Combines both models to determine the visibility of the solar and terrestrial disks, accounting for partial occultations, different solar panel orientations, tracking capabilities, mast heights, and antenna elevation masks.

4. Visualization and Analysis: Integrates the results into three modules:

  • Navigator: 3D lunar visualization, 360° horizon, polar illumination and shadow map, timeline ranging from 3 days to 1 year, and a feasibility indicator (Viable, Marginal, or Not Viable).
  • Compare: Comparison of up to four scenarios and landing ellipse sensitivity analysis using nine horizons, with offsets ranging from ±25 to ±500 m.
  • Date Planner: Heatmap of locations and dates to evaluate missions lasting 3 to 30 days and identify scenarios resilient to launch delays.

Scientific Validation and Result Reliability

The models were validated through automated tests and independent NASA reference data:

Sun and Earth Positions: Compared against JPL Horizons ephemerides (DE441, MEAN_ME frame) at equatorial and polar locations. Maximum error was below 0.005° in azimuth and elevation.

Solar Visibility: Compared against the LRO/LOLA AVGVISIB_85S_060M map, averaged over an 18.6-year nodal cycle. Across 300 random locations between 85.3°S and 89.9°S, the results achieved a correlation of r = 0.98 and an MAE of 1.1 percentage points.

Earth Visibility: Compared against the LRO/LOLA AVGVISIB_85S_060M_EARTH map using the same sampling approach. The results achieved a correlation of r = 0.99 and an MAE of 1.2 percentage points.

What Makes Sunline Different?

Sunline goes beyond displaying illumination and topographic maps: it allows users to analyze how small spatial and temporal variations affect mission feasibility.

Sensitivity Analysis: Evaluates nine points surrounding a target location to identify local variations. In certain scenarios, a small displacement can reduce solar illumination from 65% to 22%, highlighting the importance of analyzing terrain at the landing-site scale.

Optimized Processing: Incorporates a custom delta compression system for LOLA models. This reduces dataset sizes and enables horizon and illumination calculations in milliseconds, directly in the browser.

Delay-Resilient Planning: The Date Planner module allows users to anticipate how changes in launch dates affect illumination and communication, identifying locations that maintain favorable operational conditions.

Impact and Potential Applications

Sunline facilitates access to and interpretation of scientific information relevant to lunar exploration, making specialized analytical tools accessible to a broader range of users.

Preliminary Space Mission Planning: Enables comparisons of locations, dates, and operational profiles while considering the energy requirements of solar-powered rovers, the ability of hibernation-equipped modules to withstand periods of darkness, and the power and communication requirements of crewed lunar bases.

Research and Education: Allows users to interactively explore topographic shadows, polar illumination, and Earth visibility, supporting educational activities, academic projects, and preliminary research.

Open Access to Scientific Information: Provides a bilingual interface (Spanish and English), light and dark themes, an interactive guide, and shareable links that preserve simulation states. It also provides access to NASA Moon Trek, LROC QuickMap, JPL Horizons, and the Canadian Space Agency's (CSA) lunar exploration portal.

Technologies and Tools Used

The project integrates web technologies, data processing, astronomical modeling, and graphical visualization:

  • Frontend and Architecture: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Zustand, and CSS.
  • 3D Visualization and Graphics: Three.js, WebGL2, and custom GLSL shaders to render the lunar surface, LOLA terrain, and shadows.
  • Astronomical Calculations: Astronomy Engine (VSOP87/NOVAS) and the IAU WGCCRE 2015/2018 lunar orientation and libration model.
  • Processing and Validation: Python 3, NumPy, and Pillow to process and quantize LOLA PDS .IMG files; Bash and cURL to query JPL Horizons; Vitest for unit testing and reproducible statistical validation.

Considerations and Limitations

Thermal and Energy Conditions: Accounts for solar availability and continuous periods of darkness, considering conditions documented by the CSA, including lunar nights lasting approximately two weeks and temperatures reaching −200 °C.

Topographic Resolution: Horizon accuracy depends on the resolution of the digital elevation models. Annual solar illumination variations ranging from 21% to 45% were observed when comparing resolutions of 240 m and 80 m. For this reason, Sunline uses differentiated resolutions and documents its limitations.

Geographic Coverage: LOLA models cover the region between 75°S and 90°S. Outside this area, a spherical geometric horizon is used without detailed terrain reconstruction. Approximate locations of certain regions are identified with the "~" symbol.
